opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, the bar has shifted quite a bit. A few years ago, if someone could write clean, efficient code quickly, that alone was a strong signal. Now a lot of that execution layer is handled reasonably well by AI tools. You can describe what you want and get a working prototype in minutes. So raw coding speed isn't the differentiator it used to be.

What I look for now is, first, judgment: the ability to tell whether what the model produced is actually right. AI-generated code often looks plausible, and that's the dangerous part. You need someone who understands the problem deeply enough to spot a subtle bug, a wrong assumption, or an experiment that "works" for the wrong reason. In research especially, the question isn't "does it run," it's "does this result mean what we think it means."

Second, I care a lot about taste in choosing problems. When execution becomes cheap, the bottleneck moves upstream. What should we work on? What's the right question to ask? Which direction is a dead end and which one has real depth? People who can identify a good problem, frame it well, and break it into pieces that tools can help with are much more valuable than people who are just good at following instructions.

Third, first-principles thinking. I like people who don't just pattern-match to whatever is popular. They want to know *why* something works. If you only know how to call the right APIs, the AI can already do that. But if you understand the underlying mechanism, you can go beyond the existing recipes, and that's where new things come from.

And finally, curiosity and the ability to learn fast. The tools are changing every few months. The person who thrives is the one who treats AI as a collaborator, who experiments with it, figures out where it's strong and where it fails, and keeps adapting their workflow. In a sense, everyone becomes a kind of manager of very capable but unreliable assistants. The skill is knowing how to direct them, verify their work, and still own the final outcome.

So in short: less "can you write the code," more "do you know what code is worth writing, and can you tell when it's wrong."

r001.rationale: The response says taste in choosing and framing problems becomes more valuable as AI makes execution cheaper.

r002.rationale: It emphasizes deciding what to work on and which direction has depth, describing these as more valuable hiring qualities.

r003.rationale: The response values deep understanding and ownership of the final outcome, but does not identify experience combined with willingness to personally execute work as the desired profile.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a question I've been thinking about a lot, because honestly the answer has shifted in the last two or three years.

When I started hiring, a lot of the signal was about execution: can this person write a clean implementation, can they debug a distributed training job at two in the morning, do they know the tricks. Those things still matter, but they matter less, because the tools now cover a big chunk of that surface. If someone can describe a problem clearly, the model can produce a reasonable first version of the code. So raw coding throughput is no longer the thing that separates people.

What I look for now is really three things.

The first is taste. Taste in problems. Can you look at a messy space and pick the question that actually matters, rather than the one that's easiest to make progress on? The tools make it very cheap to do things, which means it's also very cheap to do the wrong things at scale. Somebody with good taste knows what not to build. That's hard to teach, and it's the thing I'd pay the most for.

The second is the ability to verify. If the model writes the code, you need to be the person who knows whether it's right. That means understanding the fundamentals deeply enough to smell when something is off, to design the experiment that would catch a bug, to not trust a plot just because it goes up. I actually think the bar on fundamentals has gone up, not down. The people who get in trouble are the ones who use the tool as a substitute for understanding instead of an amplifier of it.

The third is something like agency, or maybe stubbornness. Research is still mostly failure. The tools make the loop faster, but they don't make the problem easier, and they don't tell you to keep going when the third idea doesn't work. I want people who have a strong internal model of what they're trying to find out and will push on it.

So in interviews I spend much less time on "write this function" and much more on "here's a result, tell me why you don't believe it," or "here's a vague direction, what's the first experiment you'd run and why." The way someone reasons out loud about an ambiguous problem tells me far more than whether they can produce syntax, because syntax is now basically free.

r001.rationale: The response says AI tools make it cheap to do the wrong things at scale and that choosing which problems matter is now a highly valued quality.

r002.rationale: It says hiring priorities have shifted as AI tools cover much of execution, and emphasizes choosing meaningful questions and deciding what to investigate as qualities it now seeks.

r003.rationale: The response values agency and persistence in research, but does not identify experience combined with willingness to personally execute the work as a desired hiring profile.

astra-6.text:
I care less about how quickly someone can write code and more about whether they can figure out what’s worth building. When you have a vague problem, can you turn it into a clear question, identify the assumptions, and design a small experiment that tells you something useful?

Coding tools make execution faster, but you still need judgment. If the AI produces a solution, can you tell whether it’s correct? If an experiment gives you a surprising result, can you investigate why, rather than just accept the output?

So I look for strong fundamentals, curiosity, and ownership. You don’t have to know everything already, but you should be willing to learn, challenge your own assumptions, and keep going when the first approach doesn’t work. Someone who can use these tools and independently close that loop—from an unclear idea to a result they can explain—is very valuable.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts faster AI-assisted execution with judging what is worth building, communicating that taste matters more when coding speed is less distinguishing.

r002.rationale: It emphasizes turning vague problems into clear questions, identifying assumptions, and designing experiments, while explaining that AI speeds execution but judgment is still needed.

r003.rationale: The response values fundamentals, curiosity, ownership, and persistence, but does not identify experience as part of the desired profile.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the emphasis shifts from writing code to knowing what problem to solve. If AI can help you implement something quickly, can you identify the right question, break it down, and decide whether the result actually makes sense?

So I look for people with strong fundamentals and good judgment. When an experiment fails, can they figure out why? When the AI gives them a plausible answer, can they challenge it and find a way to test it? Producing more code doesn’t necessarily mean making more progress.

I also value curiosity and ownership. The tools keep changing, so you want someone who is willing to learn, try things, and take responsibility for the outcome. AI can accelerate that person enormously, but they still need to provide the direction.

r001.rationale: The response emphasizes identifying the right problem and using judgment, but does not clearly state that taste becomes more important in hiring.

r002.rationale: It says the emphasis shifts toward identifying the right question and concludes that people still need to provide direction when AI accelerates their work.

r003.rationale: It values curiosity, ownership, and trying things, but does not identify experience combined with willingness to personally execute work as the desired hiring profile.
